maintopic: SAFETY OF SHIPS.

speechtext:
House in Committee on Bill (No. 21) to amend the Act respecting the safety of ships-Mr. Sinclair.
On section 1,
1. Subsection 1 of section 7 of chapter 77 of the Revised Statutes, intituled An Act respecting the safety of ships and the prevention of accidents on board thereof, as amended by section 1 of chapter 63 of the statutes of 1903, is amended by striking out the words ' or in any covered space not included in the cubical contents forming the registered tonnage ' in lines 11 and 12 of the said subsection.

maintopic: SAFETY OF SHIPS.
speechtext: The purpose of the Bill is to enable sheltered deck vessels or steamers to carry timber between the main and the sheltered deck. At present they are prohibited doing so between the 12th October and 16th March. They are allowed to do so in the summer season, and I can see no good reason why they should not be permitted to fill in this space with lumber in the winter season also. The law requires of course that a ship shall not be overloaded, but the Plimsoll mark regulates that. Other descriptions of cargo are allowed between the main and the sheltered deck, but not timber, and my object is to allow the same privilege to shippers of lumber. This space consists of about eight or nine feet according to the construction of the vessel, and under the law vessels are allowed to carry only three feet of tim-her so that there are five feet not occupied at all. It would not in any way interfere with the navigation of the vessel or increase the danger to the crew if the whole space were filled up.

maintopic: SAFETY OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
It is a little difficult to hear what the hon. gentleman has said. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
I did not gather exactly what is the space to which he referred. And before he concludes his explanation, I would like to know what was the reason of the legislation in the first instance-whether or not the amendment which the hon. gentleman now proposes is in any way inconsistent with any provisions of the Imperial statutes applying to ships generally throughout the empire. I would also remark that it seems to me desirable, when a Bill of this character is proceeded with, that we should have the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in his place to give the subject his consideration. I know there has been a good deal of discussion of matters of this kind in the maritime provinces ; and while, I do not profess to have very much knowledge of the reasons pro and con. I know that there has been a difference of opinion in some quarters.

maintopic: SAFETY OF SHIPS.
speechtext: The leader of the opposition (Mr. It. L. Borden) was not in his place when I introduced the Bill. I explained that it was necessary to get the consent of the Board of Trade of England in order to have this Bill become law in Canada. I understand that the policy of the government is not to make any changes in this law unless concurred in by the Board of Trade. I laid the matter before the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and communication is now being had with the Board of Trade, to see if the proposal is satisfactory to them. I do not propose to push the Bill through its final stages until word has been received on the subject, but I would ask the House to put it through the preliminary stages, so that if the consent of the Board of Trade is obtained it can be pushed through this session. The shelter deck is a growth. It was first a roof over the deck to carry cattle. Then the roof was extended the whole length of the deck, and finally the sides were built up with the ordinary steel frame and plank, and the whole became part of the ship as much as any other part. But the law remained the same, prohibiting the carrying of timber, except to the height of three feet on the main deck. What I propose is to permit that timber be carried between the main and shelter decks, that is, eight feet above the main deck. There is no reason why it should not be allowed, especially as we permit the ship to carry cattle and other things during the winter season. There is nothing about deals or lumber to make them dangerous to carry during the winter season. We allow the ship to be filled with apples or cheese or other products, but we do not allow it to carry deals or boards except under these restrictions. It pays a certain class of ships out of business in Canada for part of the year. These vessels in the North Atlantic trade, when October 12 comes, have to go out of business because they are not allowed to carry deals in this space.

maintopic: SAFETY OF SHIPS.
speechtext: Is there any Imperial statute with the terms of which this inactment is inconsistent ?

maintopic: SAFETY OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
The Imperial statute is the same as our own which we are attempting to amend. If the amendment carried here, I presume the amendment will be made, in England similar to this.
Right Hon. Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER (Prime Minister). In the absence of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Pre-fontaine) I may explain that this matter has engaged his attention. But, as stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) it is not intended to push this Bill to a finish unless we know whether or not it is approved by the Board of Trade of England. I believe the Bill will meet with universal favour and will be a help to navigation. Still, my hon. friend only proposes to take it through committee and then let it stand until we have an answer from England.

maintopic: SAFETY OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
I am inclined to think it would be better to let the Bill remain in committee until we receive the Information from England. I do not think that will delay it at all.
Progress reported.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.

speechtext: House again in committee to consider certain proposed resolutions respecting the packing and sale of apples.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.
speechtext:
This resolution was before the Committee of the Whole a few days ago, and I think the principle was fully accepted by the House. There was, however, a doubt expressed as to whether the size of the apple box herein defined should apply only to the export trade or to internal commerce as well. I asked the committee to rise and report progress, and ask leave to sit again, for the purpose of finding out exactly what was the desire of the fruit men in this respect, and also how other parts of the Act were likely to affect them. I find that the size described for the barrels, which is already defined in the Act, is for export, and I also find that while a large number of the fruit men would be very glad to have this box defined for the internal trade also, the majority of them I think desire to take only one step at a time.

and to define the size only for the export trade. My own view is that if it is applied to the export trade, practically, the boxes made will be made for the interior trade also and they may be adopted if they wish. If anybody chooses for his own purposes to use boxes for the internal trade he can do so. Under these circumstances I wish, to amend the resolution so as to make it perfectly and absolutely clear that it applies only to the export trade, and I think that can be done by making some slight amendment in the first line of subsection 2 which reads thus :
Every person who offers or exposes for sale, or who packs for export, &c.
I think by striking out the comma after the word ' sale,' striking out the word 1 who 1 and inserting a comma after the word 'packs,' the object will be accomplished. It will then read thus :
Every person who offers or exposes for sale or packs, for export, apples, &c.
I think that will make it perfectly clear that it applies only to the export trade. The rest of the resolution indicates that it applies to the export trade only. I am informed that another amendment would be desirable. A good many people have already ordered boxes and they are being made to-day by the box-makers for the current season. The contracts have been entered into and I think under these circumstances it would be well to add a clause to this resolution saying that it shall only come into effect on, say, the first of July, 1906 instead of coming into effect on the passage of the Act. That would give full warning and give an opportunity botli to the packers and to the box-makers to adapt themselves and the conditions of their trade to the provisions of the Act as thus amended. I would therefore propose that a new clause should be added as follows :
The provisions herein contained shall come into force on the 1st July, 1906.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. minister if boxes of the dimensions mentioned in the bon. gentleman's resolution are used by other countries exporting apples to England and to what extent ?
Mr. FISHEIt. In reply to my hon. friend I would say that there are other countries which define the size of their boxes. I might say that Tasmanian apples, which are very largely used in England and which come into competition with our own apples, are packed in boxes of this size, and that this size has been found the most convenient for the trade in England. Our people have thought that by adopting the same size their apples would appeal more to the market in England than if they had a different size. This size has been found acceptable to the British trade. It is a size which has been used in British Columbia for many years and to-day a great many of the packers in 24
Ontario, at least, are using it. The fruit growers' associations of Ontario, the maritime provinces and Quebec have passed resolutions in favour of this size.

speechtext: Why do you want the word ' sale ' in at all ?

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.
speechtext:
I cannot see myself the slightest doubt as to the meaning of the words proposed. What my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) proposes is simply a different form of saying the same thing, as I understand it. I cannot see that there can be the slightest doubt as to the meaning of the words I have proposed. Sec. 4a says:
When apples are packed in Canada for export for sale by the box, &c.
The words are not exactly the same but they mean distinctly that it is only for export, and the words that I have suggested in clause b would indicate clearly that the clause as amended should only apply to the export trade. If there is any doubt about the matter or any doubt as to the wording then certainly the clause had better stand entirely as it is and we will have the law clerk of the House, or some person who is authorized to draw such clauses, draw a clause to carry out our meaning.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.
speechtext: Who has asked for this legislation ?

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.
speechtext: It has been asked for by the fruit growers' associations throughout the whole of Canada practically.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.
speechtext:
I object for my part to legislation of this kind as being altogether too paternal, and I have no doubt whatever that it will cause serious inconvenience, at any rate, in the province of Quebec and on the island of Montreal where there is an immense production of apples.
The committee will remark that this Bill comes into force only on July 1, 1906. Who knows but that the conditions of trade will be completely altered then, and so that boxes two or three inches larger will be better suited for the British trade ? I believe it is much better for a matter of this kind to be settled entirely by the usages and by the requirements of trade which are of a continually changing character. We are not going to export apples to* England only ; we may export apples to other countries where such a box as that defined in this resolution may not he a suitable box at all, and in that case the exporter will be absolutely bound by these regulations respecting the export to England. What certainty have we that within a year, apples packed differently in boxes of a different design, will not have a better sale than those packed in the box clearly defined in this resolution. I do not think this is a matter for legislation, with all due respect Mr. FITZPATRICK.
to the Fruit Growers' Association, and I think it would cause serious inconvenience to a large number of people who pack apples for export on the Island of Montreal and who will find it difficult to conform to these regulations. One of the causes given by Edwin Williams in his book on the degeneration of British trade, for that misfortune is that the English manufacturer would not conform to the requirements of the markets in the different countries with which he traded, either in the packing of goods, the making out of accounts or in the different usages of trade in the different countries. It strikes me that my hon. friend (Mr. Fisher) is here laying down a hard and fast rule for the export of apples to England. The matter would be regulated by the requirements of the trade; if the apple exporter knows that a box of the dimensions mentioned is the most suitable for the export of apples to England, he will conform to that legislation without the Dominion legislature interfering in these details.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.
speechtext:
I appreciate what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) has said, but I must tell him and tell the committee that the idea which he has promulgated here is directly contrary to what has been the growing and strong opinion of the trade. The trade, not only the apple growers but the men who pack the apples, have found it necessary to define as clearly as may be the dimensions of the pacltages'which they use. The Act that we propose to amend already contains a provision which defines the smallest barrel of apples which will be allowed in the trade. That Act w^is passed by this House deliberately after discussion, and on the demand of the apple trade, so that no smaller barrel than that particularly defined could be used. The same demand has occurred in regard to the boxes, because to-day and for some years past the box has been growing in favour as a measure or receptacle for the export trade of apples. The same requirement is needed in regard to boxes as has been adopted in regard to barrels. My hon. friend says that he wishes the usage to control the size of the box. Usage has in days gone by controlled it in regard to the barrel. Canadian apples were shipped in barrels of all sizes, and the result was that the trade in England when they ordered a thousand or
2,000	barrels of Canadian apples did not at all know how many pounds or bushels of apples they were going to get. That was one of the difficulties they had to contend with in handling Canadian apples. They expressed their dissatisfaction with that condition of affairs, and the people engaged in the trade here recognized that it was to the advantage of the Canadian trade to have a defined package so that the purchaser would know as nearly as possible what he was getting, or at any rate would know

that he was not getting less than a defined amount, and they asked that the size of the barrels should be defined. I wish to point out here that this is not an exact size but a minimum size. That is the case in regard to barrels in the Act of 1901, sec. 4, which we are about to amend. The trade has been labouring under great disadvantages by reason of the varied sizes of packages, and the trade has the minimum size defined with regard to the barrel. In the last few years the trade has found that the box is a more profitable package to use than the barrel, but the box has varying sizes. The people of Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia who have been sending apples in boxes have been using different sizes of boxes. They found that the particular box here defined was the one that was closest to the general use and that it was the best average of all those that were in use. It was also the box that was already in use in British Columbia and largely in use in Ontario. It was the box that was already in use by our chief rivals in the English apple trade, the Tasmanian shippers. The trade therefore decided, after careful consideration and discussion, and recommended by formal resolution, that this particular size of box should be adopted, and that resolution has been embodied in the proposed legislation.
I am only proposing this at the formal request of the people concerned and I think it is well that parliament should try to carry out that request. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) says that this may interfere with some people in the Island of Montreal. I may say that the fruit growers of the Island of Montreal are largely members of the Fruit Growers' Association of the province of Quebec. I could name a number of men there who are members of that association, and I have no reason to suppose that they were not quite in sympathy with the resolution passed by the Fruit Growers' Association of Quebec, asking that this should be done. Certainly if they were not in sympathy they did not go far enough to challenge the resolution because it was passed, as I understand, unanimously. Under these circumstances I feel that I am not only justified but called upon in the interests of the trade to propose a definition of the size of the box, the definition herein contained as the result of a long and full discussion. It has been adopted in the nature of a compromise, as being the box that comes nearest to all the different varieties of boxes that have been used in the past. My reason for postponing the coming into force of this amendment is simply because I am told that certain box manufacturers have already made a considerable number of the boxes for next year and a considerable number of packers have on hand boxes which they ordered for last year's crop, but which in consequence of the 24^
crop not being so large as was expected they now have on hand, and they would like to use these boxes for their next year's crop, whereas if this amendment came into force, they would not be able to use those boxes. I think that is a concession to the condition of the trade which we ought to make. But my hon. friend evidently does not understand the situation when he expresses the view that we should not to-day legislate for a box for a year hence. One of the most important things in the trade is that the packers, box-makers and fruit growers should know some little time before hand the kind of boxes they are going to use.

speechtext: I would' say to the minister that I do not intend to enter into a discussion as to whether this is the proper size for a box or not; but I would remind him that only the day before yesterday he told us that we would have time to communicate with our constituents on this matter, and now he has suddenly and, I think, rather unfairly sprung this on the committee. I think the hon. gentleman should not press this matter so hastily. He tells us that the fruit-growers have approved of this. Well, I would like to have the opinion of the fruit-growers in the county which I have the honour to represent. I know that they have an association to deal with all matters of this kind. maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OP CERTAIN COMMODITIES.
speechtext: The hon. minister is doing in this box legislation exactly what he did in the barrel legislation. In the barrel legislation he specified a minimum size, and it works like this. The cartage and the freight are exactly the same for the larger as for the smaller barrel, and when the apples are placed on the market the larger barrel has an advantage over the smaller. The reason the minimum barrel was adopted was that the manufacturers of barrels made that size and did not wish to change their machinery. The hon. gentleman is

maintopic: COMMONS '44

speechtext: pursuing a similar course with respect to the boxes. There will be two or three sizes, and the same difficulty will be experienced. Why should there not be uniform barrels and uniform boxes, so that all parties would be placed on the same footing when entering the British market ?

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext: I beg to thank the hon. member for Haiton (Mr. Henderson) for reminding me that he desired the other night to have this matter left over until he could communicate with his constituents. I had forgotten that for the moment, and I have no hesitation at all in acceding to the request that the resolutions should not be proceeded with now, and that abundant opportunity be given to all to hear from their constituents or from any others interested in the matter. At the same time, if any one wishes to make any further suggestions. I shall only be too glad to hear them before the committee rises.

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext: I wish to make this suggestion. It is possible that the Fruit-Growers' Association may have passed a resolution recommending that boxes of this size be used, and I understand that it is a matter of importance to my hon. friend to communicate the views of the association, which can be done easily through the newspapers or otherwise, to parties engaged in the export of apples. But has the association actually gone so far as to demand that a law should be passed defining the size of these boxes ? Since my hon. friend has consented to put off the consideration of this measure, I would ask him if he would have any objection to lay on the table of the House the communications of the Fruit Growers' Association ?

speechtext: Are all the apples shipped in the same sized boxes ?

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext:
No. At the present time there is no standard box. The consequence is that there is some variety in the sizes of the boxes used. The fruit-growers and the shippers have asked that we should, as far as possible, define a minimum box, so that they would not be getting smaller boxes.
Mr. OSLERt That would mean that there would be boxes of different sizes ?

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext: We expect, and it has been the result in the case of the barrel, that when a minimum is fixed, the box or barrel makers will take that as their standard, so that in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred that will be the size used. At the same time, if anybody chooses to use a larger box or barrel, he can do so.

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext: I would like to draw the minister's attention to a statement that was made by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) when this matter was under consideration before. He said that the question whether barrels or boxes were the best

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext:
*
had been considered by a commission which had been appointed in the United States, and that the report of the commission was in favour of barrels for export rather than boxes. Might I ask the hon. minister if he would be good enough to look into that, and bring before the House whatever information he can obtain on that point ?

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext: In the county which I have the honour to represent a great many apples go to waste every year, because the growers pick the apples and leave them on the ground in piles awaiting the buyers who are to classify them and put them into barrels. It has been very difficult to get barrels, and the result has been that many apples have been frozen on the ground. The farmers could make the boxes themselves and avoid delay and loss caused by waiting for barrels. It is important that this question of boxes should be settled as soon as possible. I am satisfied that many thouands of dollars' worth of apples were lost in the county I represent last year, because the farmers were not able to take care of them themselves. And I would suggest that more fruit inspectors be sent out to instruct the farmers in this matter. I would further like to suggest that some arrangement be made as soon as possible to avoid such an enormous loss. If our farmers had an idea of the size and the kind of boxes required, they would jpp doubt be in a position shortly to make the boxes themselves, and it would be well to have a standard box, not merely for export, but also for our internal trade, for we have [DOT] a great market in our own country, especially in the Northwest.

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear the remarks of the hon. gentleman. The difficulty of getting boxes and barrels in certain seasons depends largely upon the size of the crop. When there is a very large crop, the box and barrel makers are not always able to meet the demand. Unfortunately the apple crop varies very much from year to year. In some years we have an enormous crop and in other years a much smaller crop, and our box and barrel makers are at a loss to know what stock "to prepare in advance, as of course they do not care to have a large quantity left on their hands at the end of the season. As regards what my hon. friend says about teaching the farmers how to pack, my department has already taken steps in that direction. For two or three years back we have had at the exhibitions, where we could reach the fruit growing sections, an expert actually doing the work of packing apples so as to illustrate the best method. That was done in connection with the demonstration of the Fruit Marks Act, so as to teach the people how to pack the apples themselves under that Act and the best way of handling their fruit. As regards the packing

by the farmers themselves instead of selling to packers, that is a matter of trade and commerce with which I do not think the department ought to interfere. All we can do is give the people information and let them judge for themselves how they should conduct their own business.

maintopic: COMMONS '44
speechtext: I would like to point out that when there is a large stock you can easily make boxes, but not barrels. The last year or two, the packers could not get barrels on account of the difficulty of splitting staves and drying them, but boxes can be made almost while the apples are being handled.

maintopic: COMMONS '44

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext:
I wish to draw the attention of the government to an economic revolution, as it is described in ' Le Canada,' which has taken place in the United States and greatly affects our country. That revolution is in connection with the recent change made in the United States regarding drawbacks. In the ' New York Tribune ' of Sunday, February 5, there is a special from Washington dated February 4, which says :
Free hides, wool, lumber, In a word free raw and partially manufactured materials of every sort and description are now at the disposal of American manufacturers engaged in the export trade, as the result of the far-reaching drawback decision of Attorney General Moody, the text of which was published in the * Tribune ' of February 3rd.
I want to read one or two clauses from the decision. The Attorney General of the United States has given this opinion :
In my opinion, where it is proposed to export a product manufactured in the United States from a combination of domestic material and foreign material which has paid duty, and the customs officials can identify the foreign material and can ascertain to their satisfaction, by the evidence of books of account or otherwise, the quantity or measure of the foreign material actually present in the completed article, the exporter is entitled to receive a drawback of ninety-nine per cent of the duties paid upon the imported material thus ascertained to be actually present in the completed article.
And, as I have read, this is now held in-Washington to apply to every article imported into the United States for use in the production of goods to be exported. In othei words, a great revolution has taken place in the trade of that country, which vitally concerns the people of Canada. And to make still clearer what the American government is aiming* at, I wish to read a speech of the late Mr. McKinley that was quoted by the Attorney General of the United Slates and on which this recent order is based. I may say, also, that this is a reversal of two previous decisions, and is now considered to be final. The speech of Mr. McKinley in 1890 was, in part, as follows :
The Bill proposes that the American citizen may import any product he desires, manufacture it into the finished article, using in part, If necessary, in such manufacture, domestic materials, and when the completed product is entered for export, refunds to him within one per cent of all the duty he paid upon his imported materials. That is, we give to the capital and the labour of this country substantial free trade in all foreign materials for use in the

markets of the world. We do not require that the product shall be made wholly of the foreign material. Already under special provisions of laws and regulations of the Treasury Department', parts of the finished product made here and attached to the finished article does not deprive the exporter of his drawback. We have extended this provision, and in every way possible liberalized it, so that the domestic and foreign product can be combined, and still allow to the exporter ninety-nine per cent upon the duty he pays upon his foreign material intended for export ; which is, in effect, what free traders, and our political opponents are clamouring for, namely free raw material for the foreign trade. And if you are desirous of seeing what you can do in the way of entering the foreign market, here is the opportunity for you.
It completely, if the provision be adopted, disposes of what has sometimes seemed to be an almost unanswerable argument that has been presented by our friends on the other side -that if we only had free raw material we could go out and capture the markets of the world. We give them now within one per cent of free raw material, and invite them to go and capture the markets of the world.
Mr. Springer-Will the gentleman permit me to ask if that also applies to wool ?
Mr. McKinley-Yes ; it applies to anything which they choose to import for purposes of manufacture.
Here, then, is the completion of the policy as outlined by Mr. McKinley in 1890, when the tariff was revised. And it has now been sustained by the opinion of the Attorney General of the United States and put in execution by the Secretary of the Treasury. He has issued an order, dated February 4, addressed to all collectors of customs instructing them that the opinion of the Attorney General is authorized by the Treasury, and that this drawback of 99 per cent is to go into effect immediately. As I have just said this is a great revolution. The, object, as Mr. McKinley pointed out, is to capture all the foreign trade of the world. That this is a matter immediately affecting Canada is proven by the fact that the decision was given in connection with the drawback on an article imported into the United States from Canada-our wheat known as No. 1 hard. The object of the legislation as applied to that article is to allow the American millers to bring in Canadian wheat from our Northwest on the payment of a duty of 25 per cent per bushel, use it in their mills, mix it with the wheat of the United States and export the product, receiving a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty that had been paid. And what Secretary Shaw, of the Roosevelt cabinet said on that point is as follows :
It is, of course, impossible to say now just what effect this drawback ruling will have, but it will probably result in the consumption of several thousand, or perhaps several hundred thousand bushels of our domestic wheat in foreign markets that would otherwise have been thrown upon our own markets at a reduced price or not sold at all. I think it is safe to say that more than $100,000,000 worth of our Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
foreign trade to-day depends upon drawbacks for its being.
He gives an illustration bearing out this idea by showing that by reason of a drawback the American manufacturers are in a position to capture the locomotive trade of the world and that as a matter of fact, they are capturing it to-day. The correspondent of the ' Tribune ' who is very well informed-and he is evidently inspired because the ' Tribune ' is the official organ of the administration-goes on to say :
The officials of the Treasury Department do not believe that the drawback allowed on Canadian hard -wheat will cause any reduction of the customs revenue. None of that cereal is being imported now-, they say-

1 dispute that, by the' way



and the only effect that can be brought
about will be the increased sale of American soft wheat, which goes into the manufacture of exported flour. The best of the domestic wheat remains in this country and will stay here, drawback or no drawback. The cheaper grades are used with the Canadian wheat to make the flour that is demanded by the foreign trade. Heretofore these grades have not found a ready market in this country, for unless they ar* mixed with hard wheat they do not make a good bread-making flour.
The wheat raisers of the Northwest are raising some objection to a reduction in the price of the better grades of grain, and it is conceded that they have some grounds for this apprehension. But the amount of hard wheat raised on this side of the border is small, when compared with the output of the soft grain fields, and the interests benefited by the allowance are believed to be tremendously larger than those injured. The most strenuous objectors to the drawback ruling will be the millers of the Dominion of Canada. Their flour, which is now shipped to Liverpool, London, Glasgow and the other great markets of the United Kingdom, will soon meet a vigorous rival in the product that will be ground by the mills of Minneapolis, St. Paul, Chicago, St. Louis and other cities. If the American millers take away a good proportion of the trade now held by the Canadian manufacturers through the operation of the drawback concession, it may have a serious effect on the labour problem of the Dominion. If these labour interests are strong enough, it is suggested by the Treasury Department officials an effort may be made to pass an export tax law for Canada. Nothing short of such a drastic measure could interfere with the new flour trade American mills hope to acquire across the Atlantic.
Now, the trend of opinion in the United States is all in the direction of taking away from Canada the export market that we now have for our hard wheat. Our hard wheat is the best in the world. The Americans on the contrary produce any amount of wheat of lower grade. They are not in a position to export that wheat unless they can get the Canadian wheat to mix with it. But, getting the Canadian wheat, as they now propose to get it, they intend to take away the market we now have. We have a splendid and growing trade in our hard wheat and

the flour produced from it. Canadian mills 1 are doing a large and growing trade. Cam- i adian railways are carrying the product of * this wheat for export, and Canadian transportation interests get the benefit of all i freight and other charges. And Canadian workmen get all the work in connection with it. And yet we read that the policy of the American government and the American millers is to take our wheat into their country, grind it there and export it, thus depriving us of the export trade we have, depriving our railways of the business of i transporting it and our men of the wages to be earned in grinding and handling it. And they say that there is but one thing that will stop them from doing this, and that is what they call a drastic measure, namely that Canada may put on an export duty in the case of such wheat.
The other day in Montreal, at a meeting of the Board of Trade, Mr. Meighen, who is president of that body, made a statement dealing with this very question. He said there was a danger of Canada losing this trade, and he went so far as to say that he was in favour of an export duty on Canadian wheat-not so wide as had been proposed, but certainly an export duty on Canadian wheat that was to be used to be mixed with American wheat in order that a market might be found for low grade American wheat. Now is it not a matter ot national policy, a matter of extreme national peril that the government ought to consider-and it is for this reason that I direct to it the attention of the House.
Sow I am not afraid to say-I am speaking altogether for myself-that X am ready to declare myself in favour of an export duty on wheat going out of this country to be ground in the United States. X think I can give good reasons for it. First of all, the work ought to be kept in this country. In the next place, I contend that if you grind Canadian wheat in Canadian mills you get the offal, as it is called, for use in Canada for feeding cattle. Xf the wheat is exported the offal goes abroad and never comes back, but when you grind the grain in the country and sell the bran and shorts to Canadian farmers, it is used in our own country for feed and manure, and add to the productiveness of the land, and in every way the Canadian is benefited. But if you send the raw product away the country is being depleted of its natural wealth, the productiveness of the land is being reduced, and the Canadian Northwest will be brought to i the condition in which we find many of the northwestern states of the United States to-day, they are unable to produce hard wheat, and I contend that is largely due to the fact that the raw products have been sent out of that country, and no return has been made to the land to maintain its productiveness. A minister of the present government who was in the Northwest recently said, not long ago when he came
back, that the impression made upon him by his visit was that an enormous effort will have to be made by the people there if they wish to maintain the fertility of their soil, and to control the wheat market. It, has been found now that the wheat belt keeps moving north, keeps moving backwards, and the day may come when we will not have enough hard wheat of our own to mix with our own cheaper varieties. Therefore, not only is it in the interest of the Canadian workingmen and Canadian capital invested in mills, but it is in the interest of the farmer in our Northwest, that something should be done to secure the grinding of our own wheat in our own mills. I say now, notwithstanding what has been argued by some, that the Canadian farmer in the Northwest will benefit by this drawback. Perhaps for a time he will get a higher price for his product, but I contend that in the long run it will be found to be an injury. That western country is for the benefit of all Canada, and every wheat raiser in the Northwest must desire to see eastern Canada built up by these mills, and eastern workingmen kept busy, and that business may be found for our railways.
But the principle of an export duty is not confined to wheat, it touches upon and concerns a large number of other articles. Kor instance, we have in the province of Ontario the greatest supply of nickle ore in the world. To-day a large number of men are employed in developing those ores; but by reason of our present laws, and in line with the policy of the American government, we are allowing that nickle matte, that is to say, the article which has undergone the first process to be exported to the United States and refined in that country, so that for one dollar that we pay in wages here to Canadian workmen, twenty dollars are paid in wages to the United States workmen. I do not think that is in the interest of this country, and if an export duty on that nickle matte going out of this country would keep it here so that it should be refined in Canada, I think it ought to be done. Then with regard to our pulp wood, we are exporting to-day enormous quantities to the United States to be used in paper mills there, and enormous quantities are sent to the old country. Now an export duty on pulp wood would keep that industry in this country.
The Minister of Agriculture said the other day that he desired to see the cattle embargo removed from our cattle in the old country. I disagree with him there, because his policy is to have the lean cattle of Canada go into the British market. But farming is taking a new turn in these days. A good farmer does not seek simply to raise grain and sell it, but if he is wise he will raise grain and feed it to his cattle and sell only the finished product. If he is wise, the farmer, instead of selling the milk

from liis cows, will use separators and make the butter himself and use the skim-milk for feeding pigs and hens, and thereby increase his profit. The same principle runs through many other industries ; and the whole tendency is to produce the finished products in this country, even on the farm. If we in Canada can produce some finished product on a farm which will bring a higher price and furnish more labour for Can-dians, we ought to do it.
Now we come to another thing. I was reading this morning a little pamphlet of Mr. Nicholl's, of Toronto, who deals with the great development of the water-powers of Niagara. Under the law of the province of Ontario, those who are about to turn out this enormous development of electrical energy at the falls, are free to export fifty per cent of their product to the United States; so that power generated on the Canadian side of the falls, is by law, as it stands to-day, to be exjiorted into the United States, there to be used to build up immense industrial concerns. An export duty on electrical energy would prevent that. This is another instance of the new policy of encouraging commerce that has been adopted by the United States government. I say the time has come when we as Canadians, especially since we have embarked upon the national policy, ought to keep our owu markets for our own manufacturers, and our own work for our own work people. We may be forced by reason of this new policy in the United States to adopt, and extensively to adopt, the principle of export duties. It has been applied with marvellous success in the province of Ontario witli regard to saw-logs. Not long ago we exported all our saw-logs, we rafted them across the lake to mills in Michigan, where they were cut up and where American workmen, and American machinery and American capital found large profits.' But by reason of an agitation carried on in that province a change was made, and a law was passed that all the saw-logs cut off the Crown lands must be manufactured into lumber in Canadian mills.
Proposals of that kind are being made from day to day. The people are thinking about these things and to give the government some idea of what is going on and_to enable the people of the country who are interested in this new legislation in the United States to express their views I am directing attention to it to-day. The government have told the country that they are about to appoint a commission on tariff questions. I hope the powers of that commission will be wide enough to enable them to investigate matters of this kind and to go into the question of how far this new doctrine of drawbacks in the United States will affect Canadian trade. I think when they find out how extensive it is they will be very much interested. Even the shoe trade will be interested because the Arner-Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
icans have made this rule so wide that not only the leather but the shoes made from the leather of imported hides are entitled to this drawback. Woollens made in the United States from imported wool are entitled to this drawback and will come into competition with Canadian woollens. This goes all through the export trade, and therefore when the government go into this question they will find that they will not only have to take up the question of tariff revision having regard to the duties imposed under the Customs Act, but they will have to take up the question in connection with drawbacks and probably the only way to meet this new system of drawbacks in the United States is to have recourse to an export duty. One argument I have read during the last few days against the imposition of an export duty is this. In London, England, they are putting up the largest mills in the world for the grinding of flour out of Canadian wheat, and I have been asked: Would you put an export duty on wheat that goes over to the old country to be ground in London ? I would. Large mills would be worth just as much to the mother country and to Canada if they were located i on the Lake of the Woods. If we can grind i our own wheat in our own country and give work to Canadian workmen retaining the shorts and the bran for feeding Canadian cattle we ought to do so. We can do that without injuring the farmers in the Northwest Territories a single bit. I know that the great cry will be that you are going to injure the Canadian farmer in the Northwest. But, in bringing 115 the question as I do here to-day, those who represent that country and that interest will have an opportunity either now or later on to discuss the question and to present their views. I believe that the Canadian public will demand that in order to preserve our export trade and to hold our own against this new and revolutionizing policy of the United States we shall do something in this country and do it very shortly. It is simply to bring the question before the government and before the people that I take this opportunity of introducing it to the House. I would have given notice of it but I only got hold of the Montreal paper a few minutes ago with that heading on it. I am speaking altogether from my own point of view, but from a close study of the way trade is moving in this country and in other directions it is constantly coming home to us that the people of the United States, the millers, and manufacturers of the United States, assisted by a most active and progressive government and a government that is protectionist up to the hilt, have brought about a revolution in trade matters that is of the most vital interest to the people of this country.

This vote of $250,000 is to make provision towards the erection of the Victoria Memorial Museum. The contract has been let; the building is being erected on what is known in Ottawa as the Stewart property, which was acquired about two years ago for the purpose of this memorial. The building is intended to lie used for the Geological, Natural History ami Fishery Exhibits which are in

gentlemen opposite to let a contract for a building at $950,000, and say : After that is done we will put in further advertise-1 ments and call in other friends and give them a contract for the electric lighting. I suppose that is very good political policy, but I do not think it is a policy that will commend itself to the people of this country, nor do I think it a policy that will protect the public treasury.

speechtext: As to the contract for the sheds, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) knows as well as I do that that contract was let by the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. I presume the hon. gentleman desires to be fair, and, that being the case, he will admit that the question of providing electric light for a lot of iron sheds is entirely different from the lighting of a building of the character of that we are now discussing. As to what the hon. gentleman says about calling in a lot of friends of the government, he knows perfectly well that, in items such as this, the whole thing is done by tender. He knows it is all open to public competition, tencters being called for by advertisement in the public press. The whole question is one in which I must be guided by the opinion of the chief architect of the department. He has had experience, and he tells me that the plan we have adopted of calling for the main tenders first and the others afterwards is distinctly in the public interest. It is clear I could not refuse to follow the advice of the chief architect in such matters unless I had very strong evidence that he was wrong.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext:
That is not the point that we want to get at-or that I want to get at, at least. Session after session we are asked to vote sums on the strength of statements which afterwards turn out to be incorrect, and the House is led to vote sums which, if hon. members were made aware of all that was involved, probably would not be voted. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland), whom the acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) succeeded, pledged himself and the department that in all cases of new work he would place before the House the estimated cost, so that the House might know the total of the sums it would be called upon to vote for the service. But I understood the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) to say that he does not intend to carry out that underraking, but will leave the matter open, so that he can come down year after year and ask for any sums he may think well in order to carry on works that have been begun. I object to that way of doing business, and I think we have good reason to object. This is the first session of a new parliar ment, and we should understand what the course of the government is going to be in

this matter. During the recent Dominion election a really alarming state of affairs developed. We found Liberal candidates declaring that they had secured large sums of money to be expended in the constituencies for *which they sought to he elected. I think the hon. gentleman (Hr. Hyman) himself was a sinner in that respect. My opponent was able to tell me and the people that he had secured several thousands of dollars for public works in the constituency. Having the estimates before me, and having studied them pretty carefully, I found no mention of such votes. Yet this candidate could have the presumption to say that he had secured thousands to be expended in that constituency. We want that all stopped. When a public work is proposed, we want to know what is the estimated cost, in order that we may vote the money intelligently, and in order that the public may Judge intelligently the votes we give. I see some hon. gentlemen on the other side who, when they sat on this side and when we were in power, condemned in the strongest language the very things that they approve of to-day. It seems to me that before this was decided upon, the time had come for the government to consider its whole policy with regard to the harbour and the commission. Is this a bankrupt commission? Though it has paid nothing, is there no hope that it can pay anything. Sometimes it is good business policy to make advances to complete a work with the hope that out of the trade it de-velopes you may get not only interest on the last advance but interest on previous advances as well. In that way the work would have been carried on with continuity and uniformity. But this course that has been followed is evidently an expedient to relieve the Harbour Commission-or the conscience of the government I do not know which. Then the minister would not need to go to so much expense in dredging, and a part of the money now expended in that way could be utilized for docks. He can go on dredging for a hundred years, and he will not make a good harbour so long as the breakwater is kept where it is.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext:
The time may come, perhaps is fast approaching, when such an extension of the harbour will become necessary. The distance from the breakwater to the shore is not perhaps as great as it ought to be. but, at the same time, the dredging operations which are being carried on are very largely increasing the advantages of the' harbour within the breakwater. I have no doubt that the time is not far distant when the largely increased tonnage at Port Arthur and Fort William will render necessary a largely increased expenditure there. I hope to be able, at no very distant date, if I am in the Public Works Department, to
work out a more comprehensive scheme with regard to those harbours, and I intend to visit them personally along with the chief engineer of the department. Whatever plan may be determined on, this expenditure is necessary.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext: I am assured by the officers of the department that a large part of this work is being done immediately inside of the present breakwater, and that we are gradually increasing the area of deep water In time to come the larger scheme suggested by my hon. friend may be carried out.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. minister understands the point I made. The present breakwater was built when no one ever expected that vessels drawing more than 16 feet of water would enter Port Arthur harbour, but to-day it is frequented by vessels drawing 20 feet of water.	That breakwater is very close in
shore.	If this million of dollars is to be
expended in the erection of a new breakwater, at each side of the present one but much further out, undoubtedly some dredging will have to be done, but the minister cannot spend $2,000,000 honestly in dredging that harbour. What he should do is let those who are going to construct docks build them out and then a large part of the dredging could be used to fill up the eribwork and concrete work of these docks. What we want is some comprehensive scheme of building up Port Arthur and Fort William harbours. Is the hon. gentleman going to take into consideration the dredging of one of the mouths of the delta to which the leader of the opposition has referred? There are three mouths. In the middle one, dredging could be made effective for the purposes of the harbour, and if he is going to dredge the middle mouth of the delta is he going to take into consideration the fact that the value of the property in proximity to it will be greatly enhanced.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean the Mission river? There is nothing in this appropriation for the Mission river. I quite appreciate what the hon. gentleman says but it is easy in the House, when discussing harbour improvements, to speak of an expenditure of a million dollars. I would not like, however, to undertake the responsibility of any such expenditure until I had the report of the government engineers and visited the harbour personally with them. In the opinion of our engineers, the dredging we are doing will be necessary in any ease. Whether in the future we would be justified in making a large expenditure of a million or more can only be decided when we have laid out a general scheme and have ascertained whether the necessities of the harbour demand that that scheme should be carried out.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext: The matter has been before the House two or three times, but there have been so many changes in the hon. gentleman's department that the acting minister himself evidently does not know what has transpired.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext: It has been up every year since I have been in the House.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext: What I say is this, that my hon. friend cannot expend a million of dollars in dredging behind the present little breakwater in that harbour to any proper advantage.

maintopic: DRAWBACKS ON RAW MATERIALS IN THE UNITED STATES TARIFF-SUPPLY.
speechtext: I did not say it was my intention to spend any such sum there. This work covers the work in the Kaminis-tiquia river as well.
